This gives a finite, well-defined perpendicular distance between the two parallel lines (zero if they are coincident). Skew lines, by contrast, are characterised by a non-zero scalar triple product with a non-zero cross product -- both conditions must hold. The deeper lesson is that one must classify the line pair before choosing a formula: parallel lines use the parallel formula, skew lines use the skew formula, and intersecting lines have shortest distance zero by direct solution. Blindly applying a single formula without checking the cross product first is exactly the kind of error CISCE examiners flagged in the 2019 and 2023 PPA comments, where candidates "could not calculate the perpendicular distance and selected the incorrect option." Correct classification precedes correct computation.

question_text: Find the distance of the point P(2, 3, 5) from the line r = (1, 1, 1) + lambda*(1, 2, 2), giving the answer in simplified surd form.
answer_text: Use the perpendicular-distance formula d = |(p - a) x b| / |b|. Here p = (2, 3, 5), a = (1, 1, 1), b = (1, 2, 2). First compute p - a = (2 - 1, 3 - 1, 5 - 1) = (1, 2, 4). Now take the cross product (p - a) x b = (1, 2, 4) x (1, 2, 2). The i-component is 2*2 - 4*2 = 4 - 8 = -4. The j-component is 4*1 - 1*2 = 4 - 2 = 2. The k-component is 1*2 - 2*1 = 2 - 2 = 0. So the cross product is (-4, 2, 0), with magnitude sqrt(16 + 4 + 0) = sqrt(20) = 2*sqrt(5). The magnitude of b is sqrt(1 + 4 + 4) = sqrt(9) = 3. Therefore the perpendicular distance is d = 2*sqrt(5) / 3 units. This is the shortest distance from P to the line, measured along the perpendicular dropped from P to the line; any other point on the line would give a larger slant distance, which is why the cross-product formula -- not the point-to-point distance formula -- must be used.

question_text: Design a pair of skew lines whose shortest distance is exactly 2 units, and verify your construction by computing the scalar triple product and the magnitude of the cross product.
answer_text: To force the shortest distance to be 2, choose direction vectors whose cross product has a clean magnitude and a joining vector whose scalar triple product matches. Let b1 = (1, 0, 0) and b2 = (0, 1, 0); then b1 x b2 = (0, 0, 1), with magnitude 1. Choose a1 = (0, 0, 0) and a2 = (0, 0, 2), so a2 - a1 = (0, 0, 2). The scalar triple product (a2 - a1) . (b1 x b2) = (0, 0, 2) . (0, 0, 1) = 2, which is non-zero, confirming the lines are skew. The shortest distance is SD = |2| / |(0, 0, 1)| = 2 / 1 = 2 units, as required. The two lines are L1: r = (0, 0, 0) + lambda*(1, 0, 0) -- the x-axis -- and L2: r = (0, 0, 2) + mu*(0, 1, 0) -- a line parallel to the y-axis passing through (0, 0, 2). Geometrically, L1 runs along the x-axis at height z = 0, while L2 runs parallel to the y-axis at height z = 2; they never meet, are not parallel, and the vertical gap of 2 units between the two horizontal "rails" is exactly the shortest distance. This construction illustrates the bridge-and-overpass analogy: two roads at different heights passing each other perpendicularly, with the gap between them measured by the scalar-triple-product formula.

question_text: State the domain and range (principal value branch) of each of the six inverse trigonometric functions.
answer_text: sin^-^1x has domain [-1, 1] and range [-pi/2, pi/2]. cos^-^1x has domain [-1, 1] and range [0, pi]. tan^-^1x has domain R (all real numbers) and range (-pi/2, pi/2), an open interval. cot^-^1x has domain R and range (0, pi), also open. sec^-^1x has domain (-infinity, -1] union [1, infinity) and range [0, pi] \ {pi/2}, that is, [0, pi] with pi/2 removed because sec x is undefined at pi/2. cosec^-^1x has domain (-infinity, -1] union [1, infinity) and range [-pi/2, pi/2] \ {0}, with 0 removed because cosec x is undefined at 0. Each range is exactly the interval on which the original trigonometric function was restricted to make it one-to-one, and each domain is the set of values that the restricted function actually takes. Memorising the closed vs open nature of the endpoints matters: sin^-^1x and cos^-^1x have closed ranges, tan^-^1x and cot^-^1x have open ranges, and sec^-^1x and cosec^-^1x have a single point removed from an otherwise closed interval.

question_text: Explain why the trigonometric function sin x is not invertible over its full domain, and how restricting its domain to [-pi/2, pi/2] makes it invertible. Hence justify the range of sin^-^1x.
answer_text: Over its full domain R, sin x is periodic with period 2pi and is many-to-one: for instance sin(pi/6) = sin(5pi/6) = 1/2, and indeed sin(pi/6 + 2pin) = 1/2 for every integer n. A function that is not one-to-one cannot have an inverse, because the inverse would have to map 1/2 back to multiple different angles, violating the definition of a function. From node c12_math_006 we know a function is invertible iff it is bijective. To make sin x bijective we restrict its domain to [-pi/2, pi/2]. On this closed interval sin x is strictly increasing (its derivative cos x is positive on the open interior and the function is continuous on the closed interval), so it takes each value in [-1, 1] exactly once. Thus sin : [-pi/2, pi/2] -> [-1, 1] is both one-to-one and onto, hence bijective, and its inverse sin^-^1x exists with domain [-1, 1] and range [-pi/2, pi/2]. The range of sin^-^1x is precisely the restricted domain of sin x, because sin^-^1x returns the unique angle in that branch. This is why the principal value branch of sin^-^1x is [-pi/2, pi/2] and not some larger set.

question_text: A student claims that since tan x can take any real value, tan^-^1x should have range [-pi/2, pi/2] (closed) just like sin^-^1x has a closed range. Evaluate this claim, giving a balanced argument and a final judgement.
answer_text: The claim contains a correct observation but a wrong conclusion, and comparing it to sin^-^1x is misleading. The correct part is that tan x does take every real value, which is why the domain of tan^-^1x is all of R. The error is in the range. The principal branch chosen for tan x is the OPEN interval (-pi/2, pi/2), not the closed interval [-pi/2, pi/2]. The reason is that tan x is itself undefined at x = +/-pi/2 (the cosine vanishes there, so tan x = sin x/cos x has vertical asymptotes). Therefore tan x is never actually evaluated at +/-pi/2, and the restricted function maps (-pi/2, pi/2) onto R. Consequently the inverse tan^-^1x has range (-pi/2, pi/2), open at both ends: tan^-^1x can get arbitrarily close to +/-pi/2 but never equals them, because no real number x has tan x equal to +/-infinity. The contrast with sin^-^1x is instructive: sin x IS defined and equals +/-1 at the endpoints +/-pi/2 of its branch, so sin^-^1x attains +/-pi/2 (for inputs +/-1) and the range is closed. The deciding question is always whether the original trigonometric function is defined and attains its endpoint values on the chosen branch. On balance, the student's reasoning correctly links domain-of-tan to domain-of-tan^-^1 but incorrectly transfers the closed-range property of sin^-^1x to tan^-^1x without checking whether tan x is defined at the endpoints. Final judgement: the claim is incorrect; the range of tan^-^1x is the open interval (-pi/2, pi/2).

question_text: Find the principal value of each of the following: (a) sin^-^1(-1/2), (b) cos^-^1(-1/2), (c) tan^-^1(-1), (d) sec^-^1(-sqrt2). Show that each answer lies in the correct principal value branch.
answer_text: (a) We need the angle theta in [-pi/2, pi/2] with sin theta = -1/2. That angle is -pi/6, since sin(-pi/6) = -1/2 and -pi/6 in [-pi/2, pi/2]. So sin^-^1(-1/2) = -pi/6. (b) We need theta in [0, pi] with cos theta = -1/2. The angle is 2pi/3, since cos(2pi/3) = -1/2 and 2pi/3 in [0, pi]. So cos^-^1(-1/2) = 2pi/3. (Note: 4pi/3 also has cosine -1/2 but lies outside [0, pi].) (c) We need theta in (-pi/2, pi/2) with tan theta = -1. The angle is -pi/4, since tan(-pi/4) = -1 and -pi/4 in (-pi/2, pi/2). So tan^-^1(-1) = -pi/4. (d) We need theta in [0, pi] \ {pi/2} with sec theta = -sqrt2, i.e. cos theta = -1/sqrt2. The angle in [0, pi] with cosine -1/sqrt2 is 3pi/4, and 3pi/4 ~= pi/2 so it is in the branch. So sec^-^1(-sqrt2) = 3pi/4. In every case the answer lies inside the stated principal value branch, which is the defining check for a principal value.

question_text: Design a small table that, for each of the six inverse trigonometric functions, records the restricted domain of the original function, the resulting range of the inverse, the domain of the inverse, and one worked principal-value example. Then write one sentence explaining the single rule that connects all six rows.
answer_text: Table -- sin^-^1x: original sin x restricted to [-pi/2, pi/2]; range of inverse [-pi/2, pi/2]; domain of inverse [-1, 1]; example sin^-^1(1/2) = pi/6. cos^-^1x: cos x restricted to [0, pi]; range [0, pi]; domain [-1, 1]; example cos^-^1(1/2) = pi/3. tan^-^1x: tan x restricted to (-pi/2, pi/2); range (-pi/2, pi/2); domain R; example tan^-^1(1) = pi/4. cot^-^1x: cot x restricted to (0, pi); range (0, pi); domain R; example cot^-^1(1) = pi/4. sec^-^1x: sec x restricted to [0, pi] \ {pi/2}; range [0, pi] \ {pi/2}; domain (-infinity, -1] union [1, infinity); example sec^-^1(2) = pi/3. cosec^-^1x: cosec x restricted to [-pi/2, pi/2] \ {0}; range [-pi/2, pi/2] \ {0}; domain (-infinity, -1] union [1, infinity); example cosec^-^1(2) = pi/6. The single connecting rule: the range of each inverse trigonometric function equals the restricted domain of the corresponding original trigonometric function, because the inverse returns the unique angle from that restricted branch -- and the domain of the inverse equals the range (set of attained values) of the restricted original function.

question_text: Write the general Cartesian equation of a plane and state what each coefficient represents. Hence write the vector equation of a plane in terms of a position vector a and a normal n.
answer_text: The general Cartesian equation of a plane is ax + by + cz + d = 0, where (a, b, c) are the direction ratios of the normal to the plane (the vector perpendicular to the plane) and d is a constant whose value is fixed by the position of the plane in space. Specifically, if (x1, y1, z1) is a point on the plane, then d = -(a x1 + b y1 + c z1). The coefficients of x, y, z are NOT direction ratios of a line in the plane; they are the components of the normal vector n = a i + b j + c k. The vector equation of the plane is (r - a)xn = 0, where r is the position vector of any general point on the plane, a is the position vector of a fixed point on the plane, and n is the normal vector. Expanding the dot product gives the equivalent form rxn = axn, where axn is a scalar constant. For example, the plane 2x - y + 4z - 12 = 0 has normal n = 2 i - j + 4 k; a point on it is (6, 0, 0) with position vector a = 6 i, so the vector form is (r - 6 i)x(2 i - j + 4 k) = 0, or rx(2 i - j + 4 k) = 12. The two forms are interchangeable and describe the same flat surface.

question_text: A plane passes through the point (1, -2, 3) and is perpendicular to the vector 2 i + 3 j - 6 k. Derive both the Cartesian and the vector equation of this plane, and verify that the given point satisfies your Cartesian equation.
answer_text: Let the given point be A(1, -2, 3) with position vector a = i - 2 j + 3 k, and let the normal be n = 2 i + 3 j - 6 k, so the direction ratios of the normal are (a, b, c) = (2, 3, -6). For any point P(x, y, z) on the plane, the vector AP = (x-1) i + (y+2) j + (z-3) k must be perpendicular to n, so their dot product is zero: 2(x-1) + 3(y+2) - 6(z-3) = 0. Expanding: 2x - 2 + 3y + 6 - 6z + 18 = 0, which gives 2x + 3y - 6z + 22 = 0. This is the Cartesian equation. The constant d = +22, and we can confirm d = -(a x1 + b y1 + c z1) = -(2x1 + 3x(-2) + (-6)x3) = -(2 - 6 - 18) = -(-22) = +22. Verification: substitute (1, -2, 3): 2(1) + 3(-2) - 6(3) + 22 = 2 - 6 - 18 + 22 = 0. The point lies on the plane, so the equation is correct. The vector equation is (r - (i - 2 j + 3 k))x(2 i + 3 j - 6 k) = 0, equivalently rx(2 i + 3 j - 6 k) = (i - 2 j + 3 k)x(2 i + 3 j - 6 k) = 2 - 6 - 18 = -22, i.e. rx(2 i + 3 j - 6 k) = -22. Both forms describe the same plane through (1, -2, 3) perpendicular to 2 i + 3 j - 6 k.

question_text: A student is given the plane 6x - 3y + 12z = 36 and claims its normal has direction ratios (6, -3, 12) and that the equivalent vector equation is rx(6 i - 3 j + 12 k) = 36. A second student simplifies first to 2x - y + 4z = 12 and claims the normal has direction ratios (2, -1, 4) with vector equation rx(2 i - j + 4 k) = 12. Evaluate which student is correct, explaining whether the two answers represent the same plane and why simplification matters.
answer_text: Both students are technically correct about the plane itself, but the second student's answer is the better, examiner-preferred response. The two equations 6x - 3y + 12z = 36 and 2x - y + 4z = 12 are equivalent because the first is exactly three times the second -- multiplying a plane equation by any non-zero scalar yields the same plane. The normal vectors 6 i - 3 j + 12 k and 2 i - j + 4 k are parallel (one is three times the other), so they describe the same perpendicular direction, and the constants 36 and 12 are correspondingly scaled. Therefore both vector equations rx(6 i - 3 j + 12 k) = 36 and rx(2 i - j + 4 k) = 12 represent the same plane. However, the second student's approach is superior for three reasons. First, direction ratios are conventionally reported in their simplest integer form, so (2, -1, 4) is the standard answer an examiner expects; giving (6, -3, 12) without simplification can lose a mark in ICSE/JEE marking schemes that look for the "simplest form". Second, if a follow-up part asks for the unit normal or the perpendicular distance from the origin, working with (2, -1, 4) and modulus sqrt(4+1+16) = sqrt21 is far cleaner than working with (6, -3, 12) and modulus sqrt(36+9+144) = sqrt189 = 3sqrt21 -- the simplification avoids carrying an unnecessary factor of 3 through every subsequent calculation. Third, the CISCE 2019 examiner (Question 15) explicitly observed that candidates struggled with "identifying the direction ratios" and made "calculation errors" when manipulating plane equations; simplifying first is exactly the discipline that prevents these errors. The first student is not wrong about the plane, but has failed to reduce to lowest terms, which is the expected convention. The lesson: always divide the equation by the greatest common divisor of the coefficients before reading off direction ratios or writing the vector form. Both answers describe the same flat surface, but the simplified form is the canonical, mark-earning form.

question_text: Convert the vector equation rx(3 i + 4 j - 12 k) = 39 into Cartesian form. Hence state the direction ratios of the normal to the plane and identify a point that lies on the plane.
answer_text: Put r = x i + y j + z k into the vector equation rx(3 i + 4 j - 12 k) = 39. Expanding the dot product: (x i + y j + z k)x(3 i + 4 j - 12 k) = 3x + 4y - 12z. So the Cartesian equation is 3x + 4y - 12z = 39, or equivalently 3x + 4y - 12z - 39 = 0. The coefficients of x, y, z are (3, 4, -12), so the direction ratios of the normal to the plane are (3, 4, -12); the normal vector is n = 3 i + 4 j - 12 k. To find a point on the plane, set two of the variables to zero and solve for the third. Setting y = 0 and z = 0 gives 3x = 39, so x = 13; the point (13, 0, 0) lies on the plane. As a check, set x = 0, z = 0: 4y = 39 gives y = 39/4, so (0, 39/4, 0) is also on the plane. Set x = 0, y = 0: -12z = 39 gives z = -39/12 = -13/4, so (0, 0, -13/4) is also on the plane. Any of these can serve as the position vector a in the form (r - a)xn = 0. This example mirrors the CISCE 2019 Question 15 structure, where the equation 3x + 4y - 12z = 39 appeared and candidates were expected to read off the direction ratios (3, 4, -12) of the normal cleanly and without sign error.

question_text: Design a plane that passes through the point (2, -1, 4) and whose normal is parallel to the line whose direction ratios are (1, 2, 2). Write the plane's equation in both Cartesian and vector form, then construct a second, different-looking equation that represents the same plane, and explain why the two equations are equivalent.
answer_text: The normal to the plane is parallel to the line with direction ratios (1, 2, 2), so we may take n = i + 2 j + 2 k, i.e. (a, b, c) = (1, 2, 2). The plane passes through A(2, -1, 4) with position vector a = 2 i - j + 4 k. Using the one-point form a(x - x1) + b(y - y1) + c(z - z1) = 0: 1(x - 2) + 2(y + 1) + 2(z - 4) = 0. Expanding: x - 2 + 2y + 2 + 2z - 8 = 0, which simplifies to x + 2y + 2z - 8 = 0. This is the Cartesian equation. Verification: substitute (2, -1, 4): 2 + 2(-1) + 2(4) = 2 - 2 + 8 = 8, so 8 - 8 = 0. Correct. The vector equation is (r - (2 i - j + 4 k))x(i + 2 j + 2 k) = 0, or equivalently rx(i + 2 j + 2 k) = (2 i - j + 4 k)x(i + 2 j + 2 k) = 2 - 2 + 8 = 8, i.e. rx(i + 2 j + 2 k) = 8. To construct a second, different-looking equation for the same plane, multiply the entire Cartesian equation by any non-zero scalar, say 5: 5x + 10y + 10z - 40 = 0, with vector form rx(5 i + 10 j + 10 k) = 40. These are equivalent to the original because multiplying a plane equation by a non-zero scalar does not change the set of points (x, y, z) that satisfy it: every solution of x + 2y + 2z - 8 = 0 is also a solution of 5x + 10y + 10z - 40 = 0 and vice versa. The normal 5 i + 10 j + 10 k is parallel to i + 2 j + 2 k (a scalar multiple), so it specifies the same perpendicular direction, and the constant 40 is correspondingly scaled from 8. This illustrates the general principle that the equation of a plane is unique only up to a non-zero scalar multiple -- infinitely many equations describe the same flat surface, and the simplest integer-coefficient form is the conventional choice.

question_text: State the three standard forms of the equation of a plane and identify what each symbol represents.
answer_text: The three standard forms are the normal form, the intercept form, and the one-point form. The normal form is x cos alpha + y cos beta + z cos gamma = p, where (cos alpha, cos beta, cos gamma) are the direction cosines of the normal to the plane (a unit vector, so cos^2alpha + cos^2beta + cos^2gamma = 1) and p is the perpendicular distance of the plane from the origin, with p >= 0. The intercept form is x/a + y/b + z/c = 1, where a, b, c are the (non-zero) intercepts the plane makes on the x, y, z axes respectively; the plane cuts the axes at (a, 0, 0), (0, b, 0), (0, 0, c). The one-point form is a(x - x_1) + b(y - y_1) + c(z - z_1) = 0, where (x_1, y_1, z_1) is a given point on the plane and (a, b, c) are the direction ratios of the normal to the plane. Additionally, the vector form is (r - a)xn = 0, where r is the position vector of any point on the plane, a is the position vector of a fixed point on the plane, and n is the normal vector. From any Cartesian equation ax + by + cz + d = 0, the direction ratios of the normal are read off directly as (a, b, c).

question_text: Reduce the plane 3x - 4y + 12z = 39 to normal form and hence find the perpendicular distance from the origin and the direction cosines of the normal.
answer_text: The normal form is x cos alpha + y cos beta + z cos gamma = p, in which the coefficients of x, y, z must be direction cosines -- that is, a unit vector. Starting from 3x - 4y + 12z = 39, we compute the magnitude of the normal vector (3, -4, 12): sqrt(3^2 + (-4)^2 + 12^2) = sqrt(9 + 16 + 144) = sqrt169 = 13. We then divide every term of the equation by 13 (choosing the positive root because the constant 39/13 = 3 is already positive, satisfying the rule p >= 0). This gives (3/13)x - (4/13)y + (12/13)z = 3. Comparing with x cos alpha + y cos beta + z cos gamma = p, we read off cos alpha = 3/13, cos beta = -4/13, cos gamma = 12/13, and p = 3. As a check, cos^2alpha + cos^2beta + cos^2gamma = (9 + 16 + 144)/169 = 169/169 = 1, confirming the coefficients form a unit vector. Therefore the perpendicular distance of the plane from the origin is 3 units, and the direction cosines of the normal are (3/13, -4/13, 12/13). This is exactly the kind of reduction CISCE examiners flagged in 2019 (Q15) as commonly mishandled -- the key is to divide the left-hand side too, not just the constant.

question_text: A student is given the plane 2x + 3y - z = 6 and writes its intercept form as x/3 + y/2 - z/6 = 1, then states that the intercept on the z-axis is 6. Evaluate whether this answer is correct, identifying any errors and giving the fully correct version.
answer_text: The student's written equation, x/3 + y/2 - z/6 = 1, is algebraically equivalent to the correct intercept form, because -z/6 is the same as z/(-6). So the equation itself is acceptable. However, the student's claim that the intercept on the z-axis is 6 is incorrect. The intercept on the z-axis is the value of z when x = 0 and y = 0. Substituting into x/3 + y/2 - z/6 = 1 gives -z/6 = 1, so z = -6. Equivalently, reading the standard intercept form x/a + y/b + z/c = 1, the denominator c is -6, not 6. The negative sign is not a cosmetic minus in front of the term; it is part of the intercept value and carries geometric meaning -- it tells us the plane meets the z-axis on the negative side, at the point (0, 0, -6). A balanced view: the student has correctly rearranged the algebra but has misread the geometric quantity. The fully correct statement is: the intercept form is x/3 + y/2 + z/(-6) = 1 (or equivalently x/3 + y/2 - z/6 = 1), and the intercepts on the x, y, z axes are a = 3, b = 2, c = -6 respectively. The plane cuts the axes at (3, 0, 0), (0, 2, 0), and (0, 0, -6). This distinction between the algebraic form and the signed intercept is a common source of lost marks in ISC papers, because examiners specifically check whether candidates report signed intercepts. The lesson is: when asked for an intercept, always substitute the other two variables as zero and solve, rather than reading the denominator without its sign.

question_text: Find the Cartesian and vector equations of the plane passing through the point (1, 0, 2) whose normal has direction ratios (1, 2, -1). Convert your Cartesian answer to normal form and state the perpendicular distance from the origin.
answer_text: Using the one-point form a(x - x_1) + b(y - y_1) + c(z - z_1) = 0 with (x_1, y_1, z_1) = (1, 0, 2) and (a, b, c) = (1, 2, -1), we substitute directly: 1(x - 1) + 2(y - 0) - 1(z - 2) = 0. Expanding: x - 1 + 2y - z + 2 = 0, which simplifies to x + 2y - z + 1 = 0, or equivalently x + 2y - z = -1. Check: substituting (1, 0, 2) gives 1 + 0 - 2 + 1 = 0, confirming the point lies on the plane. For the vector form (r - a)xn = 0, take a = 1i + 0j + 2 k (position vector of the given point) and n = 1i + 2j - 1 k (the normal). Then (r - (i + 2 k))x(i + 2j - k) = 0, or equivalently rx(i + 2j - k) = (i + 2 k)x(i + 2j - k) = 1 + 0 - 2 = -1, i.e. rx(i + 2j - k) = -1. To convert x + 2y - z = -1 to normal form, compute sqrt(1^2 + 2^2 + (-1)^2) = sqrt6. We need the constant on the right to be positive, so rewrite as -x - 2y + z = 1 and divide by sqrt6: (-1/sqrt6)x - (2/sqrt6)y + (1/sqrt6)z = 1/sqrt6. Hence the perpendicular distance from the origin is p = 1/sqrt6 units, and the direction cosines of the normal are (-1/sqrt6, -2/sqrt6, 1/sqrt6). Note the sign flip was necessary to keep p positive.

question_text: Design a plane that cuts the coordinate axes at three points whose x- and y-intercepts are equal and whose z-intercept is the negative of the x-intercept, with the x-intercept equal to 4. Write the plane in intercept form, convert it to general Cartesian form, identify the direction ratios of the normal, and write the vector equation.
answer_text: We are told the x-intercept a = 4, the y-intercept b = a = 4, and the z-intercept c = -a = -4. So the plane cuts the axes at (4, 0, 0), (0, 4, 0), and (0, 0, -4). The intercept form is x/4 + y/4 + z/(-4) = 1, which simplifies to x/4 + y/4 - z/4 = 1. Multiplying through by 4 gives the general Cartesian form x + y - z = 4, or x + y - z - 4 = 0. From this general form ax + by + cz + d = 0 we read the direction ratios of the normal directly as (a, b, c) = (1, 1, -1). A convenient point on the plane is (4, 0, 0), with position vector a = 4i. The normal vector is n = i + j - k. The vector equation is (r - 4i)x(i + j - k) = 0, or equivalently rx(i + j - k) = 4ix(i + j - k) = 4. As a consistency check, the magnitude of the normal is sqrt(1 + 1 + 1) = sqrt3, so the perpendicular distance from the origin would be |4|/sqrt3 = 4/sqrt3 units. This constructed example illustrates how the three forms describe one and the same plane: the intercept form encodes the axis cuts, the general Cartesian form exposes the normal's direction ratios, and the vector form packages a point and a normal into a single dot-product equation.

question_text: State the formula for the perpendicular distance of a point P(x_1, y_1, z_1) from the plane ax + by + cz + d = 0, and derive the special case for the distance from the origin.
answer_text: The perpendicular distance of a point P(x_1, y_1, z_1) from the plane ax + by + cz + d = 0 is given by |ax_1 + by_1 + cz_1 + d| / sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2). The numerator is the absolute value of the expression obtained by substituting the point's coordinates into the left-hand side of the plane equation, and the denominator is the magnitude of the normal vector n = (a, b, c). For the origin O(0, 0, 0), substituting x_1 = 0, y_1 = 0, z_1 = 0 into the numerator yields |a(0) + b(0) + c(0) + d| = |d|. Therefore the distance from the origin to the plane ax + by + cz + d = 0 simplifies to |d| / sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2). This special case is zero only when d = 0, which corresponds to a plane passing through the origin. The absolute value is essential because the point may lie on either side of the plane, making the unsign ed expression positive or negative, while distance must always be non-negative.

question_text: Explain why the perpendicular distance is the shortest distance from a point to a plane, and why the absolute value is necessary in the numerator.
answer_text: The perpendicular distance is the shortest distance from a point to a plane because, of all the line segments that can be drawn from the point to various points on the plane, the one perpendicular to the plane is the unique shortest segment. Any oblique segment from the point to the plane forms the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle whose perpendicular leg is the perpendicular distance; by the Pythagorean theorem, the hypotenuse is always longer than the perpendicular leg. Hence every other segment is longer than the perpendicular distance. The absolute value in the numerator is necessary because the expression ax_1 + by_1 + cz_1 + d measures the signed quantity that depends on which side of the plane the point lies relative to the direction of the normal vector (a, b, c). If the point lies on the side toward which the normal points, the expression is positive; if it lies on the opposite side, the expression is negative. Distance, however, is a magnitude and must be non-negative regardless of side, so we take the modulus. Without the absolute value, a point on the "negative" side would yield a negative distance, which is physically meaningless and mathematically inconsistent with the definition of distance.

question_text: A student writes the plane 2x + 3y - z = 6 and computes the distance from the origin as 6 / sqrt(4 + 9 + 1) = 6/sqrt14. Evaluate whether this is correct, identify any error, and explain how the result should be obtained.
answer_text: The student's numerical answer 6/sqrt14 is numerically correct, but the reasoning contains a subtle but important conceptual slip that must be corrected to avoid errors in other problems. The plane is given as 2x + 3y - z = 6, which in the standard form ax + by + cz + d = 0 becomes 2x + 3y - z - 6 = 0. Here a = 2, b = 3, c = -1, and d = -6, not d = +6. The distance from the origin is |d| / sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2) = |-6| / sqrt(4 + 9 + 1) = 6/sqrt14. The student obtained the right magnitude only because |-6| = |6|, but the sign of d was handled incorrectly: the student treated d as +6 instead of -6. In a problem where the constant term on the right-hand side were negative, say 2x + 3y - z = -6, the standard form would be 2x + 3y - z + 6 = 0 with d = +6, and the distance would again be 6/sqrt14 -- but a student who mechanically takes the right-hand side as d would write d = -6 and still get 6/sqrt14 by luck of the modulus. The danger is that this habit breaks down when the formula is used in a larger problem, such as finding which side of the plane a point lies on, where the sign of ax_1 + by_1 + cz_1 + d matters. Therefore the correct procedure is: always rewrite the plane as ax + by + cz + d = 0 with zero on the right-hand side, read off d with its correct sign, then apply |d| / sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2). The student should be commended for the correct magnitude but corrected on the methodical handling of d's sign, because consistent procedure prevents errors in more complex questions involving signed distances, images of points, and foot-of-perpendicular problems.

question_text: Find the perpendicular distance from the point P(1, 2, 3) to the plane 2x - 3y + 6z + 5 = 0, and determine whether the point lies on the plane.
answer_text: To find the perpendicular distance from P(1, 2, 3) to the plane 2x - 3y + 6z + 5 = 0, we use the formula |ax_1 + by_1 + cz_1 + d| / sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2). Here a = 2, b = -3, c = 6, d = 5, and (x_1, y_1, z_1) = (1, 2, 3). First compute the numerator: ax_1 + by_1 + cz_1 + d = 2(1) + (-3)(2) + 6(3) + 5 = 2 - 6 + 18 + 5 = 19. Taking the absolute value gives |19| = 19. Next compute the denominator: sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2) = sqrt(2^2 + (-3)^2 + 6^2) = sqrt(4 + 9 + 36) = sqrt49 = 7. Therefore the perpendicular distance is 19/7 units, which is approximately 2.71 units. To determine whether the point lies on the plane, we check whether this distance equals zero. Since 19/7 ~= 0, the point P(1, 2, 3) does not lie on the plane. Equivalently, substituting the coordinates into the plane equation gives 2(1) - 3(2) + 6(3) + 5 = 19 ~= 0, confirming the point is not on the plane. The positive value 19 also tells us the point lies on the side of the plane toward which the normal vector (2, -3, 6) points.

question_text: Design a plane such that the perpendicular distance from the point (2, -1, 3) to it equals 5 units, and verify your construction by recomputing the distance.
answer_text: We need to construct a plane ax + by + cz + d = 0 such that |a(2) + b(-1) + c(3) + d| / sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2) = 5. Let us choose a simple normal vector, say (a, b, c) = (1, 0, 0), so the plane is of the form x + d = 0. Then the distance from (2, -1, 3) is |1(2) + 0(-1) + 0(3) + d| / sqrt(1 + 0 + 0) = |2 + d| / 1 = |2 + d|. We want this to equal 5, so |2 + d| = 5, giving d = 3 or d = -7. Choosing d = 3, the plane is x + 3 = 0. Verification: distance from (2, -1, 3) to x + 3 = 0 is |2 + 3| / sqrt1 = 5/1 = 5 units. Alternatively, choosing d = -7 gives the plane x - 7 = 0, and the distance is |2 - 7| / 1 = 5 units. Both planes are parallel to the yz-plane and lie 5 units away from the point (2, -1, 3) on opposite sides. For a richer construction, choose (a, b, c) = (2, 3, 6) with magnitude sqrt(4 + 9 + 36) = 7. The plane is 2x + 3y + 6z + d = 0. Substituting (2, -1, 3): 2(2) + 3(-1) + 6(3) + d = 4 - 3 + 18 + d = 19 + d. We need |19 + d| / 7 = 5, so |19 + d| = 35, giving d = 16 or d = -54. The plane 2x + 3y + 6z + 16 = 0 has distance |19 + 16| / 7 = 35/7 = 5 units from (2, -1, 3), verifying the construction.

question_text: State the three formulas for (i) the angle between two lines with direction ratios (a_1, b_1, c_1) and (a_2, b_2, c_2), (ii) the angle between two planes with normals (a_1, b_1, c_1) and (a_2, b_2, c_2), and (iii) the angle between a line with direction ratios (l, m, n) and a plane with normal (a, b, c). Also state the condition for a line to be parallel to a plane.
answer_text: (i) For two lines, cos theta = (a_1a_2 + b_1b_2 + c_1c_2) / [sqrt(a_1^2 + b_1^2 + c_1^2) x sqrt(a_2^2 + b_2^2 + c_2^2)]. If direction cosines (l_1, m_1, n_1) and (l_2, m_2, n_2) are given, this reduces to cos theta = l_1l_2 + m_1m_2 + n_1n_2. (ii) For two planes, the angle between them equals the angle between their normal vectors, so cos theta = (a_1a_2 + b_1b_2 + c_1c_2) / [sqrt(a_1^2 + b_1^2 + c_1^2) x sqrt(a_2^2 + b_2^2 + c_2^2)] -- structurally identical to the line formula because a plane's normal is itself a direction. (iii) For a line and a plane, sin theta = |al + bm + cn| / [sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2) x sqrt(l^2 + m^2 + n^2)], where (l, m, n) are the line's direction ratios and (a, b, c) the plane's normal. The modulus keeps theta between 0 deg  and 90 deg . The line is parallel to the plane when al + bm + cn = 0, because then the line is perpendicular to the normal and hence lies in (or parallel to) the plane. The line is perpendicular to the plane when (l, m, n) is proportional to (a, b, c), i.e. the line runs along the normal.

question_text: Two lines have direction ratios (1, 2, 3) and (-3, 2, 5). A student computes the dot product as 1x(-3) + 2x2 + 3x5 = -3 + 4 + 15 = 16 and concludes cos theta = 16/(sqrt14 x sqrt38). Explain why the method is correct, then determine whether the two lines are perpendicular, parallel, or neither.
answer_text: The student's method is correct: the dot product of the two direction-ratio vectors is indeed 16, the magnitudes are sqrt(1+4+9) = sqrt14 and sqrt(9+4+25) = sqrt38, and cos theta = 16/(sqrt14xsqrt38) = 16/sqrt532 ~= 16/23.07 ~= 0.693, giving theta ~= 46.1 deg . To decide perpendicular or parallel we check two conditions. Perpendicular requires the dot product to be zero: here it is 16 ~= 0, so the lines are not perpendicular. Parallel requires the ratios to be proportional: (1, 2, 3) = k(-3, 2, 5) would need 1 = -3k, 2 = 2k, 3 = 5k simultaneously, giving k = -1/3, k = 1, k = 3/5 -- inconsistent, so the lines are not parallel either. They are simply two oblique lines meeting at about 46 deg . This is exactly the kind of direction-ratio problem the CISCE 2019 examiner (Q17) highlighted, where students must set up dot-product equations correctly and not confuse them with cross-product conditions.

question_text: A classmate argues: "To find the angle between the planes x + y + z = 1 and 2x - y + 2z = 3, I should first find their line of intersection by solving the two equations simultaneously, then pick a point on that line and measure the angle there." Evaluate this claim, state whether the approach is sound, and give the correct method with the numerical answer.
answer_text: The classmate's claim is not sound for the purpose of finding the angle between the two planes. While it is true that two non-parallel planes intersect in a line, locating that line and "measuring an angle at a point on it" is both unnecessary and methodologically vague -- the angle between two planes is defined as the angle between their normal vectors, which is independent of any particular point of intersection and is obtained directly from the coefficients of the equations. Solving simultaneously would yield the line of intersection (reserved for the next node anyway), but it does not by itself produce the dihedral angle. The correct, efficient method is: read off the normals n_1 = (1, 1, 1) and n_2 = (2, -1, 2); compute the dot product n_1 x n_2 = 2 - 1 + 2 = 3; compute the magnitudes |n_1| = sqrt3 and |n_2| = sqrt(4+1+4) = 3; then cos theta = 3/(3sqrt3) = 1/sqrt3, so theta = cos^-^1(1/sqrt3) ~= 54.74 deg . This matches the CISCE examiner's repeated guidance (2019 Q15, 2023 Q15) that students should "clarify the concepts of dot product" and "learn different forms of plane equations and solve problems using fundamental concepts" rather than reach for elaborate side constructions. The classmate's instinct to use the intersection is understandable -- the dihedral angle is indeed measured along the line of intersection in the geometric picture -- but for computation the normal-vector dot product is the standard, fastest, and exam-expected route. A balanced view: the intersection-line picture is useful for visualising why the angle is well defined, but the calculation should always be done via the normals.

question_text: Find the angle between the line with direction ratios (1, 1, 1) and the plane 2x - y + 2z = 3. Hence state whether the line is parallel, perpendicular, or oblique to the plane.
answer_text: For a line and a plane we use the sine formula: sin theta = |al + bm + cn| / [sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2) x sqrt(l^2 + m^2 + n^2)], where (l, m, n) = (1, 1, 1) are the line's direction ratios and (a, b, c) = (2, -1, 2) is the plane's normal. The numerator is |2x1 + (-1)x1 + 2x1| = |2 - 1 + 2| = 3. The denominator is sqrt(4+1+4) x sqrt(1+1+1) = 3xsqrt3 = 3sqrt3. So sin theta = 3/(3sqrt3) = 1/sqrt3, giving theta = sin^-^1(1/sqrt3) ~= 35.26 deg . To classify: the line is parallel to the plane only if al + bm + cn = 0, but here it equals 3 ~= 0, so the line is not parallel. The line is perpendicular to the plane only if (l, m, n) is proportional to (a, b, c), i.e. (1, 1, 1) = k(2, -1, 2); this would require 1 = 2k, 1 = -k, 1 = 2k simultaneously, which is impossible (k = 1/2 and k = -1 conflict). Therefore the line is oblique to the plane, meeting it at about 35.26 deg . Note this is exactly 90 deg  - 54.74 deg , the complement of the angle between the line and the normal -- a useful cross-check.

question_text: Design a problem in which a single line is simultaneously perpendicular to two given lines with direction ratios (1, 2, 3) and (-3, 2, 5), and explain how you would find the direction ratios of the required line. Then verify your answer satisfies perpendicularity with both lines.
answer_text: To design the problem, I state: "Find the direction ratios of a line that is perpendicular to each of two lines whose direction ratios are (1, 2, 3) and (-3, 2, 5)." The method uses the fact that a line perpendicular to two given lines must have its direction vector perpendicular to both -- i.e. parallel to their cross product. Let u = (1, 2, 3) and v = (-3, 2, 5). The cross product u x v = |i  j  k; 1 2 3; -3 2 5| = i(2x5 - 3x2) - j(1x5 - 3x(-3)) + k(1x2 - 2x(-3)) = i(10 - 6) - j(5 + 9) + k(2 + 6) = (4, -14, 8). Dividing by 2 gives the simpler proportional ratios (2, -7, 4). Verification: dot with u: 2x1 + (-7)x2 + 4x3 = 2 - 14 + 12 = 0 OK. Dot with v: 2x(-3) + (-7)x2 + 4x5 = -6 - 14 + 20 = 0 OK. Both dot products vanish, so the line with direction ratios (2, -7, 4) is perpendicular to both given lines, as required. This mirrors the CISCE 2019 Q17 setup, where the examiner noted students must "let the direction ratios of the line be a, b, c" and set up the two perpendicularity equations a + 2b + 3c = 0 and -3a + 2b + 5c = 0; the cross product is the clean systematic way to solve that pair.

question_text: State the condition under which a line x = x_1 + lt, y = y_1 + mt, z = z_1 + nt is parallel to the plane ax + by + cz + d = 0, and explain the two sub-cases that arise.
answer_text: The line is parallel to the plane when al + bm + cn = 0, i.e. when the dot product of the line's direction ratios (l, m, n) with the plane's normal (a, b, c) is zero -- geometrically, the line's direction is perpendicular to the plane's normal, so the line never tilts into the plane. Two sub-cases arise. First, if additionally ax_1 + by_1 + cz_1 + d ~= 0, the base point (x_1, y_1, z_1) does not lie on the plane, so no point of the line lies on the plane: there is no intersection. Second, if ax_1 + by_1 + cz_1 + d = 0, the base point lies on the plane, and because the line is parallel to the plane, every point of the line also lies on the plane: the line is contained entirely in the plane, giving infinitely many intersection points. When al + bm + cn ~= 0, a unique intersection exists and t = -(ax_1 + by_1 + cz_1 + d)/(al + bm + cn).

question_text: The line r = (2i - j + 3k) + t(i + 2j - k) meets the plane 3x - y + z = 10. Find the parameter t and the coordinates of the intersection point, showing every step.
answer_text: First convert the vector line to Cartesian parametric form: x = 2 + t, y = -1 + 2t, z = 3 - t. The plane is 3x - y + z - 10 = 0, so a = 3, b = -1, c = 1, d = -10. Compute al + bm + cn = (3)(1) + (-1)(2) + (1)(-1) = 3 - 2 - 1 = 0. This is zero, so we must check the base point: 3(2) - (-1) + (3) - 10 = 6 + 1 + 3 - 10 = 0. Because the base point satisfies the plane equation and al + bm + cn = 0, the entire line lies in the plane -- there is no single intersection point; every point of the line is an intersection point. This illustrates the second sub-case of parallelism: the line is contained in the plane. A student who stops at "al + bm + cn = 0, so no intersection" would be wrong; checking the base point is essential.

question_text: A classmate argues: "Whenever I substitute a line into a plane and the t-terms cancel, I should immediately write 'no solution' because the line is parallel to the plane." Evaluate the correctness of this argument, giving a balanced view of when it holds and when it fails.
answer_text: The classmate's argument is partially correct but incomplete, and acting on it without further checking would lead to errors in a significant fraction of problems. The cancellation of the t-terms is indeed the algebraic signature of al + bm + cn = 0, which means the line's direction is perpendicular to the plane's normal -- the line is parallel to the plane. Up to that point the reasoning is sound. However, "parallel to the plane" does not automatically mean "no intersection." After the t-terms cancel, the equation reduces to a pure numerical statement: either a true statement such as 0 = 0 (equivalently ax_1 + by_1 + cz_1 + d = 0) or a false statement such as -3 = 5 (equivalently ax_1 + by_1 + cz_1 + d ~= 0). Only the false-statement case corresponds to no intersection. The true-statement case means the base point of the line already lies on the plane, and because the line is parallel to the plane, every point of the line lies on the plane -- the line is contained in the plane, giving infinitely many intersection points. Therefore the correct procedure is: cancel the t-terms, then inspect the remaining constant. If it is a contradiction, write "line parallel to plane, no intersection." If it is an identity, write "line lies entirely in the plane." The classmate's shortcut skips this final inspection and would misclassify the contained-line case as "no solution," losing marks. A balanced assessment: the classmate has correctly identified the first half of the test but has not completed the diagnostic, so the argument is right only in the no-intersection sub-case and wrong in the contained-line sub-case. The complete rule is al + bm + cn = 0 plus a check of the base point against the plane equation.

question_text: Find the point where the line x = 1 + 2t, y = 2 + t, z = 3 - t meets the plane x - y + 2z = 5. Hence state the value of t at the intersection.
answer_text: Substitute the parametric expressions into the plane equation: (1 + 2t) - (2 + t) + 2(3 - t) = 5. Expand: 1 + 2t - 2 - t + 6 - 2t = 5. Collect constant terms: 1 - 2 + 6 = 5. Collect t-terms: 2t - t - 2t = -t. So 5 - t = 5, giving -t = 0, hence t = 0. Back-substitute t = 0: x = 1 + 2(0) = 1, y = 2 + 0 = 2, z = 3 - 0 = 3. The intersection point is (1, 2, 3) and the parameter value is t = 0. As a check, verify the point lies on the plane: 1 - 2 + 2(3) = 1 - 2 + 6 = 5, which matches the right-hand side. The fact that t = 0 means the base point of the line itself lies on the plane -- a useful sanity check that the arithmetic is consistent.

question_text: Design a line and a plane in 3D such that the line is parallel to the plane but does not lie in it, then verify your construction by substitution. Explain how a student could systematically generate such examples.
answer_text: To construct a line parallel to a plane but not contained in it, I need al + bm + cn = 0 (parallelism) and ax_1 + by_1 + cz_1 + d ~= 0 (base point off the plane). Choose a plane first: let the plane be 2x + 3y - z = 7, so the normal is (a, b, c) = (2, 3, -1). Now pick a direction (l, m, n) perpendicular to this normal: solve 2l + 3m - n = 0. A simple choice is l = 1, m = 1, giving n = 2 + 3 = 5, so (l, m, n) = (1, 1, 5). Now choose a base point that does not lie on the plane: try (1, 0, 0); check 2(1) + 3(0) - 0 = 2 ~= 7, so the point is off the plane. The line is therefore x = 1 + t, y = 0 + t, z = 0 + 5t, i.e. r = (i + 0j + 0k) + t(i + j + 5k). Verification by substitution: 2(1 + t) + 3(t) - (5t) = 2 + 2t + 3t - 5t = 2 + 0t = 2, but the plane requires 7, so 2 = 7 is a contradiction -- no t satisfies it, confirming the line is parallel to the plane and never meets it. A student can systematically generate such examples by: (1) writing down any plane ax + by + cz + d = 0, (2) solving al + bm + cn = 0 for a direction (l, m, n) -- this is one equation in three unknowns, so there are infinitely many solutions, (3) picking any base point and adjusting the constant d so that the base point does not satisfy the plane. This recipe always yields a parallel-but-not-contained line.

question_text: Define linear programming and state the meaning of the terms objective function, constraints, and optimisation.
answer_text: Linear programming (LPP) is a mathematical technique used to find the best possible outcome -- maximum or minimum -- of a linear objective function subject to a set of linear constraints. The objective function is a linear expression in the decision variables that represents the goal of the problem, such as profit P = 40x + 30y to be maximised or cost C = 50x + 20y to be minimised. Constraints are the linear inequalities or equations that restrict the values the decision variables can take, representing real-world limits like raw material, labour hours, or budget -- for example, x + y <= 100 and x >= 0. Optimisation is the process of finding the best value (largest for maximisation, smallest for minimisation) of the objective function from among all the values permitted by the constraints. Together, these three ideas -- a goal expressed linearly, a set of linear restrictions, and the search for the best outcome -- define what a linear programming problem is.

question_text: A factory in Surat makes shirts (x) and trousers (y). Profit per shirt is Rs 200 and per trouser is Rs 150. The factory has at most 600 machine-hours, each shirt needs 2 hours and each trouser needs 3 hours. Cloth available allows at most 400 garments in total. Identify the decision variables, the objective function, and the constraints, and explain your reasoning.
answer_text: The decision variables are x (number of shirts) and y (number of trousers), because these are the quantities the factory owner can choose. The objective function is the total profit, P = 200x + 150y, which the owner wants to maximise -- this is linear in the decision variables and captures the goal in rupees. The constraints come from the two resource limits. First, the machine-hour limit: each shirt uses 2 hours and each trouser uses 3 hours, and the total cannot exceed 600, giving 2x + 3y <= 600. Second, the cloth limit: the total number of garments cannot exceed 400, giving x + y <= 400. Finally, since one cannot produce negative quantities, we add the non-negativity constraints x >= 0 and y >= 0. The reasoning is that every real-world restriction translates into a linear inequality in x and y, while the profit goal translates into the linear expression to be maximised. This is exactly the structure the CISCE 2025 examiner expected students to produce, and confusing the objective function with a constraint is the most common error reported.

question_text: A student claims that linear programming is the perfect tool for every business decision because it always gives a single best answer. Evaluate this claim, considering both the strengths and the limitations of LPP.
answer_text: The claim is overstated and incorrect in two respects: it assumes LPP applies to every business decision, and it assumes LPP always yields a single best answer. On the strength side, linear programming is indeed a powerful and widely used tool. It converts messy resource-allocation problems into a clean mathematical structure -- decision variables, a linear objective function, and linear constraints -- and it scales efficiently to problems with thousands of variables, which is why it is used in manufacturing, transportation, diet planning, and finance. It also allows "what-if" analysis by varying coefficients, helping managers test scenarios. These are genuine advantages and explain LPP's popularity in operations research. However, the limitations are substantial. First, LPP assumes that all relationships are linear; many real business situations involve non-linear effects such as bulk discounts, economies of scale, or diminishing returns, which violate this assumption and can make the LPP answer misleading. Second, LPP treats all input data -- costs, profits, resource limits -- as fixed and certain, ignoring the randomness and uncertainty that pervade real markets. Third, LPP cannot naturally handle integer-only decisions (such as "build 3 or 4 factories, not 3.7") without extensions like integer programming. Fourth, LPP ignores qualitative factors -- brand reputation, worker morale, regulatory goodwill -- that no linear expression can capture but that often drive business decisions. Fifth, the claim that LPP "always gives a single best answer" is false: when the objective function is parallel to a binding constraint, there can be infinitely many optimal solutions (as the CISCE 2025 marking scheme itself noted, "there can be infinite number of optimal solutions"), not a single one. Therefore the correct evaluation is that LPP is an excellent tool for well-structured, linear, deterministic problems, but it is not universal: it must be applied with awareness of its assumptions, and its output should be combined with qualitative judgement, not treated as the final word on every business decision.

question_text: A dietitian in a Delhi hospital must design a meal plan using rice (x kg) and dal (y kg). Each kg of rice costs Rs 40 and provides 1600 kcal; each kg of dal costs Rs 120 and provides 600 kcal and 250 g of protein. The patient needs at least 2000 kcal and at least 100 g of protein per day. State what type of LPP this is, write the objective function, and write the constraints.
answer_text: This is a minimisation problem, specifically a diet problem, because the dietitian wants the least-cost meal plan that still meets the nutritional requirements -- the goal is to minimise cost, not maximise profit. The decision variables are x (kg of rice) and y (kg of dal). The objective function is the total cost C = 40x + 120y, which must be minimised. The constraints come from the nutritional requirements. The calorie requirement gives 1600x + 600y >= 2000 (at least 2000 kcal). The protein requirement gives 250y >= 100, since only dal contributes protein in this setup, meaning y >= 0.4 kg. The non-negativity constraints x >= 0 and y >= 0 must also be included since one cannot use negative quantities of food. Note that the nutritional constraints here are "greater-than-or-equal" inequalities because the patient needs at least those amounts, unlike a manufacturing problem where resources give "less-than-or-equal" constraints. This contrast -- minimising with >= constraints versus maximising with <= constraints -- is a key feature distinguishing diet problems from manufacturing problems, and recognising it is part of mastering the terminology of LPP types.

question_text: Design your own realistic Indian LPP scenario (not a factory or a diet problem) by choosing an application area, naming the decision variables, writing an objective function, and listing at least three constraints. Explain why this is an LPP and what type it is.
answer_text: Consider a transportation problem faced by a cement company that must ship clinker from its plant in Rajasthan to two markets -- Mumbai and Delhi. Let x be the number of truckloads sent to Mumbai and y the number sent to Delhi. The cost per truckload is Rs 15,000 to Mumbai and Rs 22,000 to Delhi, so the objective function is the total transport cost C = 15000x + 22000y, which the company wants to minimise -- making this a minimisation (transportation) problem. The constraints are as follows. First, the plant can produce at most 100 truckloads in the planning period: x + y <= 100. Second, Mumbai needs at least 30 truckloads to meet demand: x >= 30. Third, Delhi needs at least 40 truckloads: y >= 40. Finally, the non-negativity constraints x >= 0 and y >= 0 apply. This is a linear programming problem because the objective function is a linear expression in the decision variables and every constraint is a linear inequality in those same variables. It is a transportation-type LPP because the underlying situation is the movement of goods from a source to destinations at minimum cost, which is one of the classic application areas of linear programming. Designing such a scenario requires identifying a real decision (how many truckloads to each city), expressing the goal linearly (total cost), and translating each real-world restriction (supply limit, demand floors) into a linear inequality -- exactly the skill this node is designed to build.

question_text: State the four steps of mathematical formulation of an LPP and write the standard form.
answer_text: The four steps are: (1) Identify the decision variables -- the unknown quantities to be decided, denoted x and y for two-variable problems, and define them in a sentence. (2) Form the objective function Z = ax + by, stating whether it is to be maximised or minimised, where a and b are the per-unit contributions of x and y respectively. (3) Express the constraints as linear inequalities (or equations) in x and y, derived from the limited resources or minimum requirements given in the problem; up to three non-trivial constraints are typical at this level. (4) Add the non-negativity restrictions x >= 0 and y >= 0, since negative values of the decision variables are meaningless in real contexts. The standard form is: Maximise (or Minimise) Z = ax + by subject to a1x + b1y (inequality) c1, a2x + b2y (inequality) c2, a3x + b3y (inequality) c3, and x >= 0, y >= 0. Each part must be present for the formulation to be complete and correct.

question_text: A furniture factory in Jodhpur makes tables and chairs. A table needs 2 units of wood and 1 hour of labour; a chair needs 1 unit of wood and 2 hours of labour. Available: 100 units of wood, 80 hours of labour. Profit per table Rs 500, per chair Rs 300. Formulate the LPP and explain why each inequality has the sign it does.
answer_text: Let x = number of tables produced, y = number of chairs produced. The objective is to maximise total profit, so the objective function is Z = 500x + 300y, to be maximised. The wood constraint is 2x + y <= 100: each table consumes 2 units of wood and each chair 1 unit, so total wood used is 2x + y, and this cannot exceed the 100 units available -- hence the "<=" sign, because using the full stock is permitted but exceeding it is not. The labour constraint is x + 2y <= 80: each table uses 1 hour and each chair 2 hours, total labour x + 2y must not exceed 80 hours, again giving "<=". The non-negativity restrictions are x >= 0, y >= 0 because the factory cannot produce a negative number of tables or chairs. The complete formulation is: Maximise Z = 500x + 300y subject to 2x + y <= 100, x + 2y <= 80, x >= 0, y >= 0. The signs "<=" arise because wood and labour are limited resources being consumed, whereas a minimum-requirement constraint such as "at least 8 units of protein" would give ">=". This distinction in the direction of the inequality is essential and is a common source of error.

question_text: A student formulates a diet problem as "Minimise Z = 2x + 3y subject to x + 2y <= 8, x >= 0, y >= 0" where the question states that the diet must contain at least 8 units of protein. Evaluate whether this formulation is correct.
answer_text: The formulation is incorrect in the direction of the constraint inequality, although the objective function and the non-negativity restrictions are correct. The question states that the diet must contain at least 8 units of protein -- this is a minimum-requirement constraint, not a limited-resource constraint. The total protein supplied by x units of food A and y units of food B is x + 2y, and this quantity must be greater than or equal to 8, so the correct constraint is x + 2y >= 8, not x + 2y <= 8. Writing "<=" would mean the diet may contain at most 8 units of protein, which is the opposite of what is required and would make the minimum-cost solution trivially zero (produce nothing), defeating the purpose of the problem. The objective function Z = 2x + 3y is correctly written because the cost per unit of food A is Rs 2 and of food B is Rs 3, and minimising total cost is the goal. The non-negativity restrictions x >= 0, y >= 0 are also correct. The error is solely in the inequality sign, but it is a fundamental one: the direction of the inequality determines whether the constraint represents a ceiling (limited resource, "<=") or a floor (minimum requirement, ">="). A balanced evaluation notes that the student has correctly identified the decision variables, the objective, and the non-negativity restrictions, but has confused a minimum-requirement constraint with a limited-resource constraint. The CISCE 2019 examiner report flagged confusion in "identifying the constraints and forming the corresponding linear inequalities," which is exactly this kind of sign error. The corrected formulation is: Minimise Z = 2x + 3y subject to x + 2y >= 8, x >= 0, y >= 0.

question_text: A manufacturer in Surat produces two types of polyester sarees, A and B. Type A requires 3 machine hours and gives a profit of Rs 40; type B requires 2 machine hours and gives a profit of Rs 30. Total machine hours available are 120. In addition, the manufacturer must produce at least 10 sarees of type B to fulfil a contract. Formulate the LPP.
answer_text: Let x = number of type A sarees produced, y = number of type B sarees produced. The objective is to maximise total profit, so the objective function is Z = 40x + 30y, to be maximised. The machine-hours constraint is 3x + 2y <= 120, because each type A saree uses 3 machine hours, each type B uses 2, and the total of 120 hours cannot be exceeded -- a limited-resource constraint giving "<=". The contract constraint is y >= 10, because at least 10 sarees of type B must be produced -- a minimum-requirement constraint giving ">=". The non-negativity restrictions are x >= 0, y >= 0. The complete formulation is: Maximise Z = 40x + 30y subject to 3x + 2y <= 120, y >= 10, x >= 0, y >= 0. This problem has two non-trivial constraints (machine hours and the contract) plus the two non-negativity restrictions, fitting within the "up to three non-trivial constraints" limit of this node. Note that the contract constraint involves only y, which is perfectly valid -- a constraint need not contain both variables.

question_text: Design your own word problem that leads to an LPP with two decision variables and exactly three non-trivial constraints (one <=, one >=, and one =), then write its full mathematical formulation.
answer_text: Word problem: A bakery in Mumbai bakes two types of cakes, chocolate (x) and vanilla (y). Each chocolate cake requires 200 g of flour and 50 g of cocoa, and sells at a profit of Rs 80. Each vanilla cake requires 100 g of flour and 30 g of butter, and sells at a profit of Rs 60. The bakery has 4 kg (4000 g) of flour available, at least 500 g of cocoa must be used to clear stock, and the bakery has a fixed order to deliver exactly 20 cakes in total. Formulate the LPP to maximise profit. Formulation: Let x = number of chocolate cakes, y = number of vanilla cakes. Maximise Z = 80x + 60y subject to the flour constraint 200x + 100y <= 4000 (limited resource, "<="), the cocoa constraint 50x >= 500 (minimum usage, ">=", noting vanilla uses no cocoa), and the fixed-order constraint x + y = 20 (exact requirement, "="), together with x >= 0, y >= 0. This gives exactly three non-trivial constraints of the three different types required: one "<=", one ">=", and one "=". The formulation is complete and ready for the graphical solution method taught in node c12_math_087.

question_text: Define the feasible region of an LPP and state the three possible classifications it can have.
answer_text: The feasible region of a Linear Programming Problem is the set of all points in the coordinate plane that satisfy every constraint (including the non-negativity restrictions x >= 0, y >= 0) simultaneously. Geometrically, it is the common intersection of all the half-planes obtained by plotting each constraint inequation. The feasible region can be classified into three types. A bounded region is a closed polygon enclosed on all sides, such as the triangle formed by x >= 0, y >= 0, x + y <= 4 with vertices (0,0), (4,0), (0,4). An unbounded region extends to infinity in at least one direction, as happens with x >= 0, y >= 0, 2x + 3y >= 6, where the region lies above the line 2x + 3y = 6 and stretches outward without closing. An infeasible region is the empty set, occurring when the half-planes have no common point -- for example the constraints x >= 5 and x <= 2 together produce no feasible point. Every point inside or on the boundary of the feasible region is a feasible solution; any point outside it is an infeasible solution.

question_text: Explain why the origin (0, 0) is used as a test point when deciding which half-plane to shade, and explain the one situation in which it cannot be used.
answer_text: The origin (0, 0) is used as a test point because substituting x = 0 and y = 0 into any linear inequation of the form ax + by <= c or ax + by >= c reduces the left-hand side to zero, making the check trivially quick: we only compare 0 with the constant c. If the inequation is satisfied, the half-plane containing the origin is the one to shade; if it is violated, the opposite half-plane is chosen. This works for the vast majority of LPP constraints encountered at the ISC level. The one situation in which the origin cannot be used is when the constraint line itself passes through the origin, that is, when the inequation is of the form ax + by <= 0 or ax + by >= 0 (for example y >= x or 2x - 3y <= 0). In that case (0, 0) lies on the line, so substituting it gives equality and does not tell us which side to shade. We then pick any other convenient point not on the line, such as (1, 0) or (0, 1), and test it instead. The reasoning principle remains the same: choose any point clearly off the line, substitute, and shade the side on which the test point satisfies the inequation.

question_text: A student plots the constraints x >= 0, y >= 0, x + y <= 4, and 2x + y >= 6 of an LPP and shades the half-plane containing the origin for every constraint. He then claims the feasible region is a bounded quadrilateral with vertices (0, 0), (4, 0), (0, 4), and (2, 2). Evaluate the correctness of his procedure and his conclusion.
answer_text: The student's procedure is flawed in two serious ways, and consequently his conclusion is also wrong. First, he has applied the "shade the origin side" rule mechanically to every constraint. For x >= 0, y >= 0, and x + y <= 4 the origin side is indeed correct, because substituting (0,0) gives 0 >= 0, 0 >= 0, and 0 <= 4, all true. However, for the constraint 2x + y >= 6, substituting the origin gives 0 >= 6, which is false. The correct half-plane is therefore the one away from the origin, not the one containing it. By shading the wrong side for this fourth constraint, the student has included points that actually violate 2x + y >= 6 and excluded points that satisfy it. Second, his claimed vertices are inconsistent. The point (2, 2) does not even lie on any of the constraint lines: 2(2) + 2 = 6 is true so it lies on 2x + y = 6, but x + y = 4 gives 4 which is on that line too -- so (2, 2) is in fact the intersection of x + y = 4 and 2x + y = 6, which is a genuine vertex. However, (0, 0) is not feasible because 2(0) + 0 = 0 is not >= 6, so it cannot be a vertex of the feasible region. Likewise (4, 0) gives 2(4) + 0 = 8 >= 6 and 4 + 0 = 4 <= 4, so it is feasible; (0, 4) gives 2(0) + 4 = 4, which is not >= 6, so (0, 4) is infeasible and is not a vertex. The true feasible region is the small triangle bounded by x + y = 4, 2x + y = 6, and the x-axis, with vertices (2, 2), (4, 0), and (3, 0). Note that (3, 0) lies on 2x + y = 6 and y = 0, and 3 + 0 = 3 <= 4, so (3, 0) is feasible; (4, 0) lies on x + y = 4 and y = 0, and 2(4) + 0 = 8 >= 6, so (4, 0) is feasible. The correct vertices are (2, 2), (3, 0), and (4, 0), giving a bounded triangular region. The lesson is that each constraint must betested individually and vertices must be computed by solving pairs of constraint equations, not guessed. This directly addresses the CISCE 2024 examiner observation that candidates "identified incorrect corner points."

question_text: Plot the constraints x >= 0, y >= 0, x + 2y <= 8, and 2x + y <= 8 on a graph. Shade the feasible region, mark its vertices, and state whether the region is bounded or unbounded.
answer_text: Begin by drawing the coordinate axes, which represent the constraints x >= 0 (right of and including the y-axis) and y >= 0 (above and including the x-axis); together they confine us to the first quadrant. Next, plot the line x + 2y = 8. Its intercepts are (8, 0) when y = 0 and (0, 4) when x = 0; draw a solid line through these points. Test the origin: 0 + 2(0) = 0 <= 8, true, so shade the half-plane containing the origin, that is, below and to the left of the line. Then plot 2x + y = 8 with intercepts (4, 0) and (0, 4); draw a solid line. Test the origin: 2(0) + 0 = 0 <= 8, true, so again shade the origin side. The feasible region is the common overlap in the first quadrant: a quadrilateral bounded by the two slanted lines and the two axes. Its vertices are found by solving pairs of equations simultaneously: (0, 0) from the axes; (4, 0) from 2x + y = 8 with y = 0; (0, 4) from x + 2y = 8 with x = 0; and the intersection of x + 2y = 8 and 2x + y = 8, which subtracting gives x - y = 0, so x = y, and substituting gives 3x = 8, hence x = y = 8/3, giving the vertex (8/3, 8/3). The feasible region is therefore a bounded quadrilateral with vertices (0, 0), (4, 0), (8/3, 8/3), and (0, 4). Because it is a closed polygon entirely enclosed, we classify it as a bounded feasible region.

question_text: Design your own two-variable LPP arising from a real-life Indian context (for example, a small factory in Surat producing two types of garments) with at least three constraints. Write the formulation, describe how you would graph it, and predict the shape of the feasible region without actually computing the vertices.
answer_text: Consider a small garment factory in Surat that produces two types of shirts: type A requiring 2 hours of cutting and 1 hour of stitching per piece, and type B requiring 1 hour of cutting and 2 hours of stitching per piece. The factory has available at most 8 hours of cutting time and 8 hours of stitching time per day, and obviously cannot produce negative quantities. Let x denote the number of type A shirts and y the number of type B shirts produced per day. The constraints are: 2x + y <= 8 (cutting time), x + 2y <= 8 (stitching time), x >= 0, y >= 0 (non-negativity). To graph this, I would first draw the coordinate axes for x >= 0 and y >= 0, confining the picture to the first quadrant. Then I would plot the line 2x + y = 8 through the intercepts (4, 0) and (0, 8) as a solid line, test the origin (0 + 0 = 0 <= 8, true), and shade the origin side. Next I would plot x + 2y = 8 through (8, 0) and (0, 4), test the origin (true again), and shade the origin side. The feasible region is the common overlap of these four half-planes. Without computing the vertices exactly, I can predict the shape: because both resource lines have negative slopes and both pass through the first quadrant, and because both origin-side half-planes are kept, the feasible region will be a bounded quadrilateral with one vertex at the origin, one on the x-axis where 2x + y = 8 meets y = 0, one on the y-axis where x + 2y = 8 meets x = 0, and one interior vertex where the two slanted lines cross. The region is bounded because all four boundary lines close it off -- there is no direction in which a feasible point can travel to infinity while still satisfying both <= constraints. This prediction matches the structure of the worked example in Q4, confirming that the region is a bounded quadrilateral.

question_text: State the fundamental theorem of linear programming and explain the corner point method for finding the optimal feasible solution.
answer_text: The fundamental theorem of linear programming states that if an optimal feasible solution to an LPP exists, then it is attained at one of the vertices (corner points) of the feasible region. The corner point method exploits this: first, plot all the constraints (including x >= 0, y >= 0) and shade the feasible region. Second, identify every corner point of this region by solving each pair of boundary lines simultaneously. Third, evaluate the objective function Z = ax + by at each corner point. Fourth, compare the values: for a bounded region, the largest value is the maximum and the smallest is the minimum, and both always exist. For an unbounded region, after finding the candidate value at a corner, check the open half-plane of the objective line to confirm no better value lies deeper in the unbounded part. The corner point and its Z-value together constitute the optimal feasible solution. This method works because Z is linear, so its extreme values on a convex polygonal region occur at extreme points (vertices), never in the interior.

question_text: Maximize Z = 3x + 4y subject to x + y <= 4, x + 3y <= 6, x >= 0, y >= 0 using the corner point method. Show all working.
answer_text: First, identify the boundary lines: L1: x + y = 4, L2: x + 3y = 6, plus the axes x = 0 and y = 0. Find their intersections. L1 and L2: subtracting gives 2y = 2, so y = 1, x = 3, corner (3, 1). L1 with y = 0: x = 4, corner (4, 0). L2 with x = 0: 3y = 6, y = 2, corner (0, 2). The axes meet at (0, 0). So the bounded feasible region has vertices (0, 0), (4, 0), (3, 1), (0, 2). Now evaluate Z = 3x + 4y at each: Z(0,0) = 0; Z(4,0) = 12; Z(3,1) = 9 + 4 = 13; Z(0,2) = 8. Comparing, the maximum is 13 at (3, 1) and the minimum is 0 at (0, 0). Because the region is bounded, both optima exist and are guaranteed to be at vertices. The optimal feasible solution for maximization is therefore Z_max = 13 at the point (3, 1). The reasoning hinges on the theorem that a linear function on a closed bounded polygon attains its extrema at corner points, so testing all four corners is sufficient and no interior point need be checked.

question_text: A student solves an LPP with an unbounded feasible region and declares "Since the region is unbounded, no optimal solution exists." Evaluate the correctness of this claim, giving a balanced argument with a counter-example.
answer_text: The student's claim is over-generalised and therefore incorrect as a blanket statement. It is true that an unbounded feasible region can fail to have an optimum -- for example, maximizing Z = x + y over the region x + y >= 5, x >= 0, y >= 0 (the first-quadrant area on and above the line x + y = 5) gives no maximum, because points like (100, 0), (1000, 0) keep increasing Z without limit. In that specific direction the optimum does not exist, and the student would be right. However, the same region can have a perfectly well-defined minimum: minimizing Z = 2x + 3y over x + y >= 5, x >= 0, y >= 0 gives corner points (5, 0) and (0, 5), with Z values 10 and 15 respectively, and the open half-plane 2x + 3y < 10 lies entirely outside the feasible region, so no feasible point gives a smaller Z -- the minimum Z = 10 at (5, 0) exists. This counter-example shows that an unbounded region can have an optimum in one direction (minimization) while lacking one in the other (maximization). The correct procedure is therefore: evaluate Z at all corner points to get a candidate optimum, then check whether the open half-plane of the objective line, in the direction of optimization, intersects the feasible region. If it does not, the candidate is the true optimum; if it does, no optimum exists in that direction. The student's error is to treat "unbounded" as automatically equivalent to "no optimum," ignoring the directional check. A balanced conclusion: unboundedness is a warning flag, not a verdict -- it tells you to verify, not to abandon the search. CISCE examiners (PPA 2019) noted that candidates frequently mishandle unbounded regions, so this verification step is exactly what is being tested.

question_text: A manufacturer makes two products A and B. Profit per unit is Rs 40 on A and Rs 30 on B. Constraints: 2x + y <= 100 (machine hours), x + y <= 80 (labour), x >= 0, y >= 0, where x = units of A, y = units of B. Find the optimal product mix that maximizes profit.
answer_text: The objective function is Z = 40x + 30y (profit in rupees). The constraints are 2x + y <= 100, x + y <= 80, x >= 0, y >= 0. Find the corner points. Boundary lines L1: 2x + y = 100 and L2: x + y = 80. Subtracting L2 from L1 gives x = 20, then y = 60, so intersection is (20, 60). L1 with y = 0: x = 50, corner (50, 0). L2 with x = 0: y = 80, corner (0, 80). L1 with x = 0: y = 100, but check L2: 0 + 100 = 100 > 80, so (0, 100) is infeasible; the correct axis corner on L2 is (0, 80). The axes meet at (0, 0). So the bounded feasible region has vertices (0, 0), (50, 0), (20, 60), (0, 80). Evaluate Z: Z(0,0) = 0; Z(50,0) = 2000; Z(20,60) = 800 + 1800 = 2600; Z(0,80) = 2400. The maximum profit is Rs 2600, attained at x = 20, y = 60. The optimal product mix is 20 units of A and 60 units of B. The region is bounded, so this is the guaranteed global maximum.

question_text: Design your own LPP word problem involving two products and three non-trivial constraints (besides non-negativity), where the objective function turns out to be parallel to one of the binding constraints, producing infinitely many optimal solutions. State the problem, the formulation, and demonstrate the multiple optima.
answer_text: Problem: A bakery in Delhi makes two types of sweets -- gulab jamun (x boxes) and rasgulla (y boxes). Profit is Rs 50 per box on each. Constraints: each box of gulab jamun uses 2 kg of milk and each box of rasgulla uses 2 kg of milk; total milk available is 100 kg, so 2x + 2y <= 100, i.e. x + y <= 50. Each box of gulab jamun needs 1 hour of preparation and each box of rasgulla needs 1 hour; total preparation time is 50 hours, so x + y <= 50 (the same as the milk constraint -- to force parallelism, use sugar instead: each box uses 1 kg sugar and total sugar is 50 kg, giving x + y <= 50 again). To get a genuinely distinct third constraint, add: gulab jamun boxes need 3 g of saffron each, rasgulla need 1 g, total saffron 90 g, so 3x + y <= 90. Non-negativity: x >= 0, y >= 0. Objective: maximize Z = 50x + 50y. The binding constraint x + y <= 50 is parallel to the objective function Z = 50x + 50y (both have slope -1). Corner points: (0, 0); (30, 0) from 3x + y = 90 with y = 0; intersection of x + y = 50 and 3x + y = 90 gives 2x = 40, x = 20, y = 30, corner (20, 30); (0, 50) from x + y = 50 with x = 0 (check 3(0) + 50 = 50 <= 90, feasible). Evaluate Z: Z(0,0) = 0; Z(30,0) = 1500; Z(20,30) = 1000 + 1500 = 2500; Z(0,50) = 2500. Both (20, 30) and (0, 50) give Z = 2500, and because the objective line is parallel to the edge x + y = 50 joining them, every point on that segment is also optimal. Hence there are infinitely many optimal feasible solutions, all lying on x + y = 50 between (0, 50) and (20, 30), each giving maximum profit Rs 2500. This mirrors the CISCE 2025 specimen pattern where Z = px + qy is maximized at two corners, forcing the conclusion p = q and infinitely many optima.

question_text: State the definition of conditional probability P(A|B), including the condition on P(B), and explain what the reduced sample space means.
answer_text: Conditional probability P(A|B) is the probability that event A occurs given that event B has already occurred. It is defined as P(A|B) = P(AintersectionB) / P(B), provided P(B) > 0 (because we cannot condition on an impossible event). The reduced sample space is the set of outcomes belonging to B -- once we know B has occurred, every outcome outside B is ruled out, so the universe of possible outcomes shrinks from the original sample space S to B itself. Within this reduced space, the favourable outcomes for A are those that lie in both A and B, i.e. in AintersectionB. Therefore the conditional probability is the ratio of the number (or probability) of AintersectionB outcomes to the number (or probability) of B outcomes. For example, if S = {1,2,3,4,5,6}, B = {4,5,6} (number > 3) and A = {2,4,6} (even), then the reduced space is {4,5,6} with 3 outcomes, of which {4,6} are even, so P(A|B) = 2/3. Using the formula: P(AintersectionB) = 2/6 = 1/3 and P(B) = 3/6 = 1/2, giving (1/3)/(1/2) = 2/3. The two methods agree because both capture the same idea of restricting attention to B.

question_text: Two cards are drawn successively without replacement from a standard 52-card deck. Let B be "the first card is a king" and A be "the second card is a king". Compute P(A|B) and P(A), and use them to determine whether A and B are independent.
answer_text: After the first card (a king) is drawn and not replaced, the deck contains 51 cards of which 3 are kings. Hence the reduced sample space for the second draw has 51 outcomes with 3 favourable, so P(A|B) = 3/51 = 1/17 ~= 0.0588. Without any conditioning, the probability that the second card is a king is P(A) = 4/52 = 1/13 ~= 0.0769 (by symmetry, the second card is equally likely to be any of the 52 original cards). Since P(A|B) = 1/17 ~= 1/13 = P(A), the occurrence of B has changed the probability of A, so A and B are dependent events. We can confirm with the product test: P(AintersectionB) = P(B)xP(A|B) = (4/52)(3/51) = 12/2652 = 1/221, whereas P(A)xP(B) = (4/52)(4/52) = 16/2704 = 1/169. Since 1/221 ~= 1/169, independence fails. This is the hallmark of sampling without replacement: each draw alters the composition of the remaining set, making successive draws dependent. The student must always state the reduced deck (51 cards, 3 kings) before computing, as CISCE examiners expect this explicit step.

question_text: A student claims, "If two events are mutually exclusive, they must be independent, because they do not overlap and therefore do not affect each other." Evaluate this claim, explaining the relationship between mutual exclusivity and independence with a numerical example.
answer_text: The claim is fundamentally incorrect and reflects a confusion that CISCE examiners have repeatedly flagged (2019 PPA: candidates confused "mutually exclusive and independent events"). In fact, mutually exclusive events (other than impossible ones) are maximally dependent, not independent.
